A) N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW
B) N, NW, W, SW, S, SE, E, NE

D) N, NE, NW, E, W, SE, SW, S
a

Exactly right — moving clockwise from North you pass through NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, and NW before returning to North. Now let's connect compass points to actual bearing numbers on a map.

When using a protractor to measure the bearing between two map locations, which line on the map should be aligned with the protractor's baseline?
A) The latitude line (running east–west)
B) The longitude line (running north–south)
C) The north line or meridian on the map
D) The scale bar of the map
c

Exactly — you always align the north line first, then measure clockwise to your target. That's the anchor for every bearing calculation.

A geography field study requires students to record directions from a survey point to four landmarks. The students measure bearings of 030°, 120°, 210°, and 300°. Which pair of bearings represents locations that are directly opposite each other?
A) 030° and 120°
B) 120° and 300°
C) 030° and 210°
D) 210° and 300°
c

Exactly — opposite bearings differ by 180°, and 030° + 180° = 210°. Now let's convert a compass point to a bearing directly.

What is the bearing equivalent of the compass point Southwest (SW)?
A) 135°
B) 225°
C) 315°
D) 45°
b

A) Slightly south of east (E-SE)
B) Slightly south of due south (S-SE)
C) Slightly east of due south (S-SE)
D) Slightly east of due east (E-SE)
c

B) 180°
C) 450°
D) 360°

d

360 degrees is like a full circle right

Exactly — one full turn is always 360°, no matter how many angles you split it into around that point. Now let's apply it: four angles around a point measure 70°, 50°, 90°, and x°.

A) 150°
B) -30°
C) 30°
D) 120°

ok so i add them up. 70 plus 50 is 120, then plus 90 is 210. so 360 minus 210 is 150.

a

Five angles around a point are 80°, 80°, 70°, 70°, and e°. What is e?
A) 120°
B) 60°
C) -120°
D) 390°

ok so 80 plus 80 is 160, then 70 plus 70 is 140. so 160 plus 140 is 300. then 360 minus 300 is 60.

b

B) 170°
C) 50°
D) 120°

ok so 50 plus 80 is 130, then plus 60 is 190, then plus 50 is 240. so 360 minus 240 is 120.

d

A) 155°
B) -75°

D) 105°

ok so 75 plus 85 is 160, then plus 95 is 255. so 360 minus 255 is 105.

d
Five angles around a point measure 50°, 55°, 70°, 65°, and y. Calculate y.

ok so 50 plus 55 is 105, then plus 70 is 175, then plus 65 is 240. so 360 minus 240 is 120.

y is 120 degrees
On a straight line, angle A is 120°. What is the supplementary angle?
wait, what do you mean by supplementary? is that like angles on a straight line?

Exactly — supplementary means two angles that add up to 180°, which is exactly the rule for angles on a straight line. So if angle A is 120°, its supplementary angle is whatever's left to make the pair total 180°. Given that, what is the supplementary angle to 120°?

oh ok so 180 minus 120 is 60.

so the supplementary angle is 60 degrees
One angle on a straight line is 140°. Find the other angle.

180 minus 140 is 40.

so the other angle is 40 degrees

Exactly right — 180° − 140° = 40°. Now let's check two angles at once on a line.

Two angles on a straight line are 150° and 30°. What is their sum?

150 plus 30 is 180.

yeah that makes sense because they're on a straight line

Exactly — angles on a straight line always add to 180°, that's the linear pair rule. Now let's stretch to a full circle: at a roundabout in Victoria, four roads create angles of 85°, 92°, 88°, and x around the centre.

At a roundabout in Victoria, Seychelles, roads branch off in four directions creating four angles around the central point. The angles measure 85°, 92°, 88°, and x. Find x to determine all angles at the roundabout.

ok so 85 plus 92 is 177, then plus 88 is 265. so 360 minus 265 is 95.

x is 95 degrees

A) 270°
B) 180°
C) 450°
D) 360°
D

Exactly — 360° is the total, every time, no matter how many angles share that point. Now apply it: Four angles around a point measure 70°, 50°, 90°, and x°. What is x? A) 150° B) -30° C) 30° D) 120°

A) 150°
B) -30°
C) 30°
D) 120°

70 plus 50 plus 90 is 210, so 360 minus 210 is 150.

A

Five angles around a point are 80°, 80°, 70°, 70°, and e°. What is e?
A) 120°
B) 60°
C) -120°
D) 390°

80 plus 80 plus 70 plus 70 is 300, so 360 minus 300 is 60.

B

Five angles around a point are 50°, 80°, 60°, 50°, and m°. Find m.
A) 240°
B) 170°
C) 50°
D) 120°

50 plus 80 plus 60 plus 50 is 240, so 360 minus 240 is 120.

D

Three angles around a point are 80°, 50°, and x°. What is x?
A) 130°
B) 40°
C) 230°
D) 50°

80 plus 50 is 130, so 360 minus 130 is 230.

C

Exactly right — 230°. Now let's push it further with five angles instead of three.

Five angles around a point measure 50°, 55°, 70°, 65°, and y. Calculate y.

50 plus 55 plus 70 plus 65 is 240, so 360 minus 240 is 120.

y is 120°

Exactly right — 120° closes the full circle around the point.

Which statement is true?
A) Angles around a point sum to 180°
B) Angles on a straight line sum to 180°
C) Any three angles always sum to 360°
D) Two angles on a straight line are always equal
B

Exactly right — angles on a straight line always sum to 180°.

Now try this: Three angles sit on a straight line. Two angles measure 45° and 65°. What is the third angle?

45 plus 65 is 110, so 180 minus 110 is 70.

the third angle is 70°

D

B) 72°

360 divided by 5 is 72.

Let's start with the basics. **What does a map scale of 1:25,000 indicate?** A) 1 centimetre on the map represents 25,000 centimetres on the ground B) 1 metre on the map represents 25,000 metres on the ground C) 25,000 maps are needed to cover the ground area D) The map covers an area of 25,000 square kilometres

A) 1 centimetre on the map represents 25,000 centimetres on the ground
B) 1 metre on the map represents 25,000 metres on the ground
C) 25,000 maps are needed to cover the ground area
D) The map covers an area of 25,000 square kilometres
b

Not quite — map scales are almost always written using the smaller unit, centimetres, since that's what you'd measure with a ruler on paper. Think about the number "25,000" as telling you how many of that SAME small unit fit into the real-world distance — which unit from the options is that?
ohh wait, so its a then? 1 centimetre on the map is 25,000 centimetres on the ground

Exactly — 1 cm on the map equals 25,000 cm on the ground, which converts to 250 m in real life. Now let's apply this to a real distance measurement.

A student measures a straight line on a map using a ruler and gets 5 cm. However, they forget to record the map scale. Without the scale, why is the measurement essentially useless?
A) The measurement will always be inaccurate
B) Without the scale, the ground distance cannot be determined
C) The scale will change if the map is photocopied
D) Rulers are not reliable measurement tools
d

Not quite — rulers themselves are fine tools, so that's not the issue here. Think about what the scale actually does: it's the link between the centimetres you measure and the real distance on the ground — without it, what can you actually calculate from that 5 cm?
ohh right, so its b then? without the scale you cant figure out what the ground distance is cause you dont know how many times bigger it is

On a map with a scale of 1:200,000, a measured distance of 3 cm represents how many kilometres on the ground?
A) 3 km
B) 6 km
C) 20 km
D) 60 km
6 km

Exactly — 3 cm × 200,000 = 600,000 cm, which converts to 6 km. Now let's check a trickier one involving unit conversion errors.

A student converts 8.5 cm on a 1:200,000 map to ground distance and gets 1,700 km. What error has been made?
A) The student forgot to convert centimetres to kilometres
B) The student used the wrong map scale
C) The student multiplied instead of dividing
D) The student misread the ruler by 0.5 cm
a

Which tool would be most appropriate for measuring the length of a winding mountain path on a map?
A) A ruler
B) A string or piece of thread
C) A compass
D) A protractor
a

A ruler only measures straight lines well, but this mountain path winds and curves a lot. Think about which tool can bend and follow curves before you straighten it out to read the length against a ruler — which option fits that description?
ohh wait, its b then? you use the string to follow the curvy path and then measure the string with a ruler

Exactly — you lay the string along all the curves and bends of the path, then pull it straight and read its length off the ruler, which converts a wiggly distance into a straight measurable one. That's precisely why a string beats a rigid ruler for this job. Go ahead and select that option now to lock in your answer.
yeah b, string or piece of thread
